title: The War Widens
subtitle: Northern counterattacks, Odessa and violence behind the front
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: Soviet counterattacks south of Lake Ilmen and Odessa’s continuing sea connection imposed different demands on the invading armies. Civilian work, Romanian persecution and SS cavalry killing operations reveal the wider human geography of the August campaign.
body:
The Soviet plan for 12 August gave the 11th Army two tasks around Staraya Russa: recover ground and prevent German formations from moving against its neighbours. The second task could matter even if the first failed. South of Lake Ilmen, a counterattack might oblige the Germans to divert troops from their advance towards Leningrad. The plan therefore measured success partly in forces kept elsewhere, while specifying the rivers, bridgeheads and formations through which the army was expected to fight its way forward. [1]a

Hundreds of kilometres to the south, Odessa posed another problem of commitment. Romania’s 4th Army approached a port that the Soviet command required to hold, with the Black Sea Fleet maintaining a connection after the land routes closed. The two battles demanded different means, but both complicated an invasion still seeking decisive results. Their costs reached beyond formations in combat. Civilians built defences, sustained workshops and sought evacuation, while German and Romanian occupation extended persecution across communities behind the advancing front. [2]b

The northern offensive encounters a system of defences

Army Group North’s advance toward Leningrad involved three connected but distinct tasks. Georg von Küchler’s 18th Army had to clear the Baltic coastal region and Estonia. Erich Hoepner’s 4th Panzer Group supplied the principal mobile striking force toward Leningrad. Ernst Busch’s 16th Army protected the eastern side of the advance, including the region around Lake Ilmen. The army group’s commander, Wilhelm Ritter von Leeb, could concentrate on the city only if these operations supported one another. A successful thrust northward that left Soviet forces on its southeastern flank would lengthen vulnerable communications while reducing the troops available to protect them. [3]

The Luga region gave the defenders time and a series of positions through which to contest the approaches to Leningrad. Forests and difficult ground restricted movement, increasing the value of roads and crossings. During July, the Soviet command strengthened the defence while German infantry approached the leading armour. The renewed German attack therefore faced an opponent with more preparation than the rapid initial advance had allowed. A breakthrough still offered major possibilities, but it had to be exploited through routes on which artillery, engineers and supply columns also depended. The north’s problem was becoming a sustained battle for access to the city. [4]

The renewed offensive broadened during the second week of August. Blau’s operational account dates the general three-pronged effort to 10 August, distinguishing the advance north from the Ilmen region, the attack from the Luga area, and the western approach. These were converging operations, not three columns moving at a common speed. The formations encountered different defensive positions and could not exchange support freely across the intervening terrain. In particular, an advance toward Novgorod, at the northern end of Lake Ilmen, had implications for the eastern communications of the Luga defenders as well as for the route farther north. [4]

The Soviet northern defence also faced pressure from Finland. The Finnish offensive on the Karelian Isthmus had begun on 31 July, while operations east of Lake Ladoga created another demand on Soviet forces. German expectations that the Finns would advance promptly toward the Svir underestimated the problems of their exposed flank and Soviet forces in the Lake Onega region. Finland’s campaign was related to German strategy, but it did not operate as a mechanically synchronised northern pincer. On both sides, the availability of units in one sector depended on decisions and resistance elsewhere. [4]c

Staraya Russa and the vulnerable flank

South of Lake Ilmen, the fighting around Staraya Russa exposed the practical meaning of flank protection. The town connected roads and railways through a region divided by the Lovat, Polist, Redya and smaller rivers. Soviet troops east and south of the town could threaten German communications supporting the advance farther north. For the German 16th Army, control of the town therefore required more than possession of its buildings. Forces had to hold the approaches, keep crossings usable, and prevent a Soviet thrust from turning the rear of the units already committed around it. [1]

The 11th Army’s journal records the pressure on the other side of that campaign. On 3 August, German attacks along the Shimsk road and near the railway prompted Soviet efforts to restore the position. Aircraft damaged the line near Pola station, cut wires from Staraya Russa and bombed the army command post three times. Requests for fighter protection had not been met. These entries place the headquarters inside the battle it was trying to direct. Its staff needed reports from threatened units while air attacks damaged the means of receiving them. [1]

The journal’s account for 4 August attributed German success to artillery, mortars and effective cooperation between aircraft and ground troops, while acknowledging the failure of some Soviet units to hold. This was an interested explanation by a command assessing its reverses, but its detail identifies the mechanisms at work. Fire disrupted formations, damaged communications and complicated movement behind the line. The same entry described Staraya Russa burning under long-range artillery bombardment. The town’s role as a junction connected the military effort to civilian exposure: routes needed for reinforcement and supply also concentrated danger around the places through which inhabitants moved. [1]

By 10 August the situation had deteriorated further. The German thrust along the Staraya Russa–Ramushevo road had disorganised the 254th Rifle Division, whose commander was reported to have lost control by the evening. Its withdrawal toward the Lovat created an urgent need to restore order before renewed offensive action. The sequence is revealing: the counterattack of 12 August was not being prepared by an army resting intact behind a secure line. Some of the formations assigned to attack were simultaneously recovering from defeat, rebuilding communications and trying to retain the crossings through which their next movement would pass. [1]d

Seven tanks in an army’s daily record

The 11th Army journal recorded seven KV tanks arriving for the 163rd Division on 3 August. On the fourth it listed eight KVs available to army command and their employment with the 22nd Rifle Corps. These are separate dated entries, not numbers to combine into a single strength return. They show scarce heavy tanks being assigned while headquarters moved infantry and requested air cover across threatened sectors.[1]e

The counterstroke of 12 August

The plan signed by Vasily Morozov, the 11th Army commander, and his staff prescribed a main attack on the army’s left toward Mavrino and Vyachkovo. The 254th Rifle Division and the 163rd and 202nd motorised formations were assigned to this effort, with the 21st Motorised Rifle Regiment following. A supporting attack by the 22nd Rifle Corps would move from the Parfino direction toward Staraya Russa. The 180th and 183rd Rifle Divisions were to lead there, while the 182nd followed along the main road. This distribution sought to apply pressure across the German position rather than feed every available formation into one narrow approach. [1]

The timetable connected successive river problems to the recovery of Staraya Russa. It called for the Redya line on 12 August, further positions including the Porusya on the thirteenth, the town’s eastern part and the Polist on the fourteenth, and the town and Dolzhitsy front by the end of the fifteenth. These remained ordered stages. Each assumed that the preceding crossing could continue serving troops and supplies as the leading formations moved on. The schedule therefore exposes the depth of coordination required from an army whose starting positions were unsettled and whose communications had already suffered serious damage. [1]

The second-echelon formations had a dual responsibility. They were to hold bridgeheads and protect crossings successively on the Lovat, Redya, Polist and Porusya, while also reinforcing the attack when circumstances permitted. That assignment connected the forward battle with supply. An attacking regiment could cross a river before its artillery, ammunition transport or casualty evacuation arrangements were secure. Leaving troops at the crossings reduced the immediate striking force but protected the means of sustaining it. The order recognised this tension explicitly. It also left final divisional tasks dependent on the fighting of 11 August, an acknowledgment that the starting position itself was still unsettled. [1]f

The larger counterstroke involved the 34th Army moving into the gap south of Staraya Russa while the 11th fixed German troops around the town. Robert Forczyk’s account identifies a gap of approximately forty-eight kilometres between the German X and II Corps and describes the resulting danger to the 30th and 290th Infantry Divisions. German commanders responded by sending Erich von Manstein’s LVI Motorised Corps, including the SS Totenkopf formation, against the penetration. The German counterattack began on 19 August. Its success subsequently forced Soviet troops back toward the Lovat. These later events establish both the seriousness of the Soviet threat and its limits; they were not completed outcomes on the study’s anchor date. [5]

The Soviet operation affected the sequence of German action even though its gains were not retained. Mobile formations were redirected to restore communications and secure the flank of the northern advance, and Hitler ordered an armoured corps transferred from Army Group Centre in response to the danger. Resources considered for a renewed central effort were consequently drawn into another sector’s emergency. The operational effect lay in compelling this redistribution and the fighting required to make the northern position usable again. It must be weighed alongside the Soviet losses incurred when the German response developed, rather than treated as an uncomplicated success measured solely by the diversion achieved. [4]g

From the Dniester toward Odessa

In the south, the destruction of the Soviet grouping around Uman had altered the balance without resolving the campaign. As the previous study explains, the final resistance there continued beyond the date attached to many accounts of the German victory. Farther south, the Southern Front had to withdraw while preserving enough cohesion to defend new positions. The coastal army protecting Odessa faced a separate requirement: remain near the port while neighbouring forces moved away. Its commander, Georgy Sofronov, could not simply match the retreat of the rest of the front without abandoning the task Moscow had assigned. [3] [2]

Romania’s 4th Army under Nicolae Ciupercă approached from the Dniester region. Its movement toward Odessa carried the war beyond the recovery of territories lost by Romania to the Soviet Union in 1940. Romanian forces remained participants in the Axis campaign, with their own command structure and the political ambitions of Ion Antonescu shaping their employment. The operational directive issued on 8 August ordered the 4th Army to defeat Soviet forces between the Dniester and the Tiligul estuary and occupy Odessa. The distance to the objective could be covered more quickly than the defending army could be destroyed. [6]h

Romania’s advance brought a programme of persecution. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum documents army and gendarmerie killings during the reconquest of Bessarabia and northern Bukovina, independently and alongside German units. In Kishinev, German and Romanian forces shot Jews in July; approximately 11,000 survivors were confined in a ghetto and subjected to forced labour. The advance beyond the Dniester extended Romanian occupation farther east. Later deportations must retain their own dates.[15]i

The cost of the approach was already visible at regimental level. Colonel Raoul Halunga’s 10th Vânători Regiment, in the 15th Infantry Division, had crossed the Dniester and fought around Sibka in early August. A museum study based partly on his surviving service documents records repeated Soviet counterattacks and substantial losses in this period. His regiment’s experience demonstrates why the phrase “advance on Odessa” should not imply an uninterrupted march. The fighting before the city’s principal defensive positions consumed the same infantry and leadership that would be needed for the assault. [6]j

The relationship between retreat and defence can be followed in the Southern Front’s own orders. Directive 0049/op prescribed a staged withdrawal, an intermediate line to be reached by 10 August and a more distant line by the twelfth. It instructed the Coastal Army to begin its withdrawal on the night of 7–8 August toward Berezovka, Katarzhino, Razdelnaya and the Kuchurgan estuary, covered by strong rearguards. The same document required the removal of weapons and equipment from the Rybnitsa and Tiraspol fortified regions. Moving soldiers eastward was only part of the task; valuable matériel also had to be recovered before the roads and crossings disappeared. [7]

Guns left behind could not strengthen the next line; guns moved too soon might leave the rearguard without support. The document’s staged timetable addressed this dilemma by prescribing successive positions and covering forces. It records an effort to preserve an army during retreat, rather than a guarantee that each stage was completed. This distinction is particularly important near Odessa, where one command was expected to continue defending while neighbouring forces withdrew farther east. [7]k

A port could remain connected after its land routes closed

Stavka’s directive of 5 August had rejected Budenny’s proposed withdrawal line on the Ingul and specified a more forward position. It also distinguished the immediate withdrawal line from a deeper defensive line, some one hundred to one hundred and fifty kilometres farther back. This was an attempt to preserve space and time rather than surrender both in a single movement. Within that instruction, Odessa received an exceptional obligation: it was to be defended to the limit, with the Black Sea Fleet involved. The port would remain a defended projection west of the larger Soviet withdrawal. [2]

Rear Admiral Gavriil Zhukov commanded the Odessa naval base, while Vice Admiral Filipp Oktyabrsky commanded the Black Sea Fleet. Sofronov’s army and the naval establishment consequently had related responsibilities under different immediate chains of command. The distinction mattered because the defence required coastal artillery, ships, infantry, transport and port facilities to work together. On 19 August, a week after this study’s anchor date, the Odessa Defence Region would place the combined local defence under Zhukov. That later reorganisation should not be read backward as an arrangement already fully in place on 12 August. [8]

The ELAR account dates the final closure along the coast to 13 August. On the twelfth, isolation was still developing. Closing the land routes did not sever Odessa’s sea connection with the Soviet war effort. That distinction explains how the city could continue receiving support while neighbouring armies withdrew east.[9][4]

The contrast with Uman rests on that surviving connection. The armies trapped inland had to request ammunition by air as their room for receiving it contracted. Odessa retained a port through which the fleet could help sustain a defended position. The difference explains the possibility of continued resistance, without proving that every shipment arrived or every civilian could obtain passage. [10] [2]l

Civilian work and civilian exposure

The 11th Army journal describes Staraya Russa burning under bombardment. Artillery covered entrances and exits used by troops, exposing residents travelling for food, seeking relatives or trying to leave. A damaged railway could obstruct military supply and civilian flight at once. Escape could become dangerous well before every road was closed; the record does not supply a precise evacuation total.[1]m

Odessa’s civilians also constructed defences and kept workshops operating. That labour connected the garrison’s endurance to households facing bombing and decisions about evacuation. The existence of a sea route must be distinguished from a particular family’s access to it: military transport capacity alone does not establish how many civilians could leave, or when they could do so. [9]n

Production and family life

A room beside his father’s workshop

In his February 2003 Centropa interview, Mikhail Gauzner remembered his father remaining in Odessa with workers making mine housings after the main plant’s evacuation. As bombing increased, Mikhail and his mother moved into a small room beside his father’s office. His childhood recollection gives no exact date for the move. It connects continuing production with a family’s effort to find shelter and remain together.[11]o

For the Gauzners, defensive work and family safety came to depend on the same workplace. His father’s decision to remain affected where his wife and son could shelter. Their particular experience restores one Jewish household to the city’s defence before occupation and persecution transformed its circumstances; it cannot establish every resident’s motives or opportunities.

A report signed by SS cavalry officer Franz Magill on 12 August reveals another use of military organisation behind the front. Covering operations in the Pripyat marshes from 27 July to 11 August, it reported no experience of battle, yet claimed thousands of killings under the language of combating “looters”. It also described an attempt to drive women and children into marshes to drown them, which failed because the water was too shallow and the ground firm. The document’s terminology concealed the anti-Jewish operation; its detail exposes the perpetrators’ purpose. The reported total of 6,526 was the unit report’s claim, not an independently verified total for the entire SS cavalry campaign. [16]p

Strategy and the international supply question

On 12 August Hitler issued a supplement to Directive 34. Army Group South was to prevent a continuous Soviet defensive line on the Dnieper, seize Crimea and pursue the industrial regions around the Donets and Kharkov. Army Group Centre was to eliminate dangerous flank positions and rehabilitate its armoured forces before an offensive toward Moscow. The northern operation received a decisive place in this sequence: the Leningrad battle was to be brought to a successful conclusion, and the VIII Air Corps returned to the central sector, before the Moscow offensive began. The directive offered conditional opportunities whose requirements competed with one another. [4]

Aircraft had to be allocated among competing operations. The German supplement assigned priorities, while the Soviet 11th Army journal described unanswered requests for fighter cover. These opposing records do not explain one another’s allocation decisions. For troops under attack, the practical test was whether protection arrived while a road, railway or command post could still be defended.[4][1]q

Western diplomacy was beginning to turn the Soviet supply problem into an international undertaking, although promises still preceded deliveries. Roosevelt and Churchill met at the Atlantic Conference on 9–12 August. Their joint message proposing further consultation on Soviet needs reached Stalin through the American and British ambassadors on 15 August. The timing matters: these diplomatic steps could influence expectations and procurement, but they could not have equipped the counterattacking armies at Staraya Russa three days earlier. Britain was already a belligerent against Germany; the United States was assisting resistance to the Axis while remaining outside formal war with Germany. [12]

Stalin’s comments to the ambassadors on 15 August connected the southern battlefield with that diplomatic effort. He acknowledged severe strain in Ukraine and anticipated the loss of Nikolaev. His statements about the total number of enemy divisions and comparative aircraft and tank strength were contemporary claims, not verified statistical balances. More concretely, he requested armour plate and aluminium and argued that Arkhangelsk offered advantages over Vladivostok, citing the Japanese complication and the long Trans-Siberian railway journey. Even the form in which aid should be supplied depended on transportation: shipping material for Soviet manufacture might be more practical than moving complete heavy vehicles. [13] [14]r

What widening meant on 12 August

By 12 August, German success in the south and renewed effort in the north were producing further battles rather than a single conclusion. Staraya Russa threatened the flank of the Leningrad advance. Odessa could remain connected by sea after Romanian forces reached the coast. The rear areas, meanwhile, were becoming sites of organised persecution whose victims were absent from ordinary combat-strength calculations. The widening war required attention to these different processes: reinforcement and diversion at the front, civilian work within defended cities, and killing by military and police organisations behind the advance.

The northern counterattack and Odessa’s defence remained unresolved, while the junction at Gomel was coming under greater pressure. Its roads and rivers linked the central and southern theatres. The next study follows the loss of the city, the effort to rebuild an army beyond it, and the civilian routes used before occupation.[4]s

sourceMethod: This study integrates the proofread manuscript’s Part III with the existing web account. Lettered evidence notes retain detailed references and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the source register. Published Soviet transcriptions distinguish orders from reported results; their archival references do not imply inspection of original files. Contemporary claims, later testimony and historical interpretation remain attributed. The update is a manuscript reconciliation, not a new independent audit of every cited source. The dated map retains its own feature sources and precision notes.
editorialRevision: Updated the existing web study from Part III of Ostkrieg Volume One version 3.3.22; all associated asides and native endnotes reconciled. Existing URLs, section IDs and historical map data preserved.
